questions.stem: You are running a charter boat in Canadian waters when the Coast Guard relays a signal that a person is in distress nearby. What does the Canada Shipping Act, 2001 require of you?
options: Wait for the Coast Guard to confirm that you have been requisitioned before you alter course to assist
Proceed with all speed to assist and, if possible, inform the persons in distress or the sender
Proceed only if the signal came directly from the vessel in distress, not as a relay
Continue the voyage and report the signal in the log book at the end of the day
questions.explanation: Section 131(1) applies on receiving a signal from any source, so a relay counts. You do not wait to be requisitioned, and you do not need the call to come from the casualty itself.

questions.stem: A master decides, in the special circumstances, that it is unreasonable to go to a distress call. What must the master do?
options: Nothing; no record is required
Ask the casualty's master to sign a release
Enter the reason in the vessel's official log book
Obtain a written release from the Minister of Transport
questions.explanation: Section 131(2) excuses the master but requires the reason to be entered in the official log book. No release is needed from anyone.

questions.stem: What is a requisition under s. 131?
options: A master asks the Minister for permission to stop assisting a vessel in distress
A search and rescue coordinator orders a vessel to leave the search area and stand by
The distressed vessel's master calls on answering vessels to assist, and they must keep going
The authorized representative recalls the vessel to port to protect its crew
questions.explanation: The power in s. 131(3) belongs to the master of the vessel in distress. A requisitioned vessel keeps going all speed; it cannot use the other vessel's arrival as an excuse until released under s. 131(4) or (5).

questions.stem: Which of these releases a master from the duty to proceed to a vessel in distress?
options: The persons in distress tell the master that assistance is no longer necessary
The master's passengers ask to return to port before the vessel arrives
The master hears that a larger vessel might be somewhere in the area
The weather forecast gets worse and the master is worried about the safety of the crew
questions.explanation: Section 131(5) releases a master told by the persons in distress, or by the master of another vessel that has reached them, that assistance is no longer necessary. A worse forecast or a passenger request is not a release; the s. 131(2) exit is for being unable, or finding it unreasonable or unnecessary, and then logging the reason.

questions.stem: Under s. 131(4), when is a master released from the duty to proceed?
options: When the master has travelled half the distance to the casualty
When the master learns that another vessel is complying with a requisition
When the casualty's authorized representative has been notified of the distress
When the master reaches Canadian waters on the way to the casualty
questions.explanation: Section 131(4) releases the master on learning that another vessel is complying with the requisition. Distance and waters are irrelevant.

questions.stem: You find a person in the water at sea who seems in danger of being lost, with no distress call made. Does the Act require you to help?
options: Yes, but only if the person in the water is a Canadian citizen or permanent resident
No, only a received distress signal creates a duty to give assistance
Yes, the master must assist every person found at sea in danger of being lost
Yes, but only if your vessel is more than 15 gross tonnage and certified
questions.explanation: Section 132 is independent of any signal. Nationality and the size of your vessel do not matter.

questions.stem: Two vessels collide in fog. Each master is unhurt and neither vessel is sinking. Which statement about the Act's duties is correct?
options: The duties apply only if someone on either vessel is injured in the collision
The masters must exchange only the vessels' names, and only if asked to do so
Only the master of the give-way vessel has these duties, since that vessel caused the collision
Both must stand by and give the vessel's name and the representative's name and address
questions.explanation: Section 148 puts both duties on the master or person in charge of each vessel. The assistance duty lasts until the other master has determined no further assistance is needed, and the information duty (name, authorized representative's name and address, other prescribed information) is separate and applies regardless of injuries.

questions.stem: After a collision, what limits a master's duty to render assistance to the other vessel?
options: The master need only help if the other master asks for help in writing or by radio
The master need only help if the other vessel is the smaller of the two
Only so far as it can be done without endangering the master's own vessel, crew or passengers
There is no limit; the master must stay even if their own vessel is sinking
questions.explanation: Section 148 opens with 'if and in so far as they can do so without endangering their vessel, crew or passengers'. The size of the vessels and any written request are not part of the test.

questions.stem: A search and rescue mission coordinator directs you by radio, while you are in Canadian waters, to join a search for an overdue kayaker. What is your position?
options: You may refuse if the direction is not in writing
You must comply only if you hold a master's certificate
You must comply only if you are within 25 nautical miles of the search area
You must comply with the direction
questions.explanation: Under s. 130(2) a coordinator may direct any vessel to take part in a search or otherwise render assistance, and s. 130(3) says every vessel and person on board in Canadian waters shall comply. The Act does not require writing or a certain distance.

questions.stem: Which duty has the higher maximum fine under the Act?
options: Failing to give your vessel's name and authorized representative after a collision, up to $1,000,000
Failing to render assistance after a collision, up to $1,000,000 or 18 months or both
Failing to log the reason for not answering a distress call, up to $500,000
Both carry the same maximum
questions.explanation: Section 151 covers failing to render assistance after a collision (up to $1,000,000 or 18 months, or both). Section 152 covers failing to give the information and has a maximum of $25,000.
